strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation across seven benchmarks spanning structured grids, unstructured PEBI meshes, nested LGR hierarchies, and dynamic mesh optimization (DMO) point clouds, covering single-phase, multipase, compositional, and thermal physics.

The central capability claim — direct learning from adaptive-mesh datasets with time-varying topology and node counts without interpolation — is convincingly demonstrated (Table 3, 4x error reduction over interpolated baselines) and is genuinely valuable for the subsurface community where DMO/LGR data are common but unusable by grid-based operators.

Strong baselines including prior SOTA on the respective datasets (MGN-LSTM checkpoints from Ju et al. 2024, Nested FNO checkpoints from Wen et al. 2023), plus ablations isolating the fused vs. local-only vs. global-only encoder (Tables 1, 3, 4, 14).

Honest and nuanced discussion of limitations: the super-resolution section (4.1) correctly distinguishes architectural mesh-invariance from training-data mesh convergence, and openly reports that APT degrades on the heterogeneous ATES dataset; the CarBench reproduction caveats are transparently documented.
Good reproducibility detail: full hyperparameters, optimizer, GPU memory, training throughput, and per-dataset training costs (Tables 7, 8, 12); datasets promised for release.

Interesting empirical findings beyond raw accuracy: cross-dataset joint training boosting a data-limited task from R^2 32% to 86.7% (Table 6) and OOD generalization to unseen geostatistical classes (Table 14).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty. APT is largely an assembly of existing components: Perceiver-style cross-attention, GNN message passing with radius pooling, gated feature fusion (which the authors themselves admit has been explored in prior hybrid operators), DiT-style conditioning, and cross-attention decoding. The claimed novelty reduces to applying the fused representation as the latent token, which is an incremental design choice rather than a new mechanism.

Theoretical justification is thin. The claim that the global branch 'mimics integral operator behaviors' while the local branch 'adheres to the sparsity inherent in differential operators' is asserted but never analyzed or substantiated; there is no analysis of when/why the gate G allocates capacity between branches beyond qualitative ablation deltas.

Some ablation gains are marginal relative to the framing: on ATES the fused model improves relative L2 only from 0.014 to 0.011, and on CarBench Table 5 the differences are within reported standard deviations, yet the paper titles the fusion a key architectural contribution.

Comparisons are not always apples-to-apples: in Table 4 Nested FNO achieves better saturation error (1.46% vs 2.5%) and the advantage is reframed as a 'trade-off'; grid baselines on the ATES benchmark pay an interpolation penalty by construction. On CarBench (Table 13) APT ranks second behind AB-UPT with notably higher variance, slightly softening the 'outperforms SOTA' claims in the abstract.

The 'first to learn directly from adaptive mesh refinement' claim is difficult to verify; graph-based simulators (MeshGraphNet variants) can in principle consume dynamic meshes, and the paper does not compare against a graph-simulation baseline on the DMO dataset, instead arguing they 'fail to make prediction' without direct evidence.

Several results lack uncertainty quantification or are based on small subsets (e.g., 5 representative test meshes for the faulted CO2 case), and the autoregressive stability of the model over long horizons — a known failure mode of one-step-trained operators — is only partially addressed via the hydrocarbon extrapolation test.
Code is only promised upon publication; given the many dataset-specific implementation variants, reproducibility currently rests entirely on the appendix descriptions.

strengths: The evaluation is unusually broad: seven datasets spanning structured, unstructured, adaptive, and nested-LGR meshes, multiple physics regimes (multiphase flow, compositional flow, heat transfer), plus an OOD test and a cross-dataset training experiment. The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including training costs (Tables 7-8) and runtime comparisons.

The problem domain is significant, and the core architectural motivation (subsurface media are strongly heterogeneous, so purely global attention or purely local message passing each miss part of the physics) is reasonable and clearly argued.

The Discussion (Section 4.1) is refreshingly honest about the limits of super-resolution in subsurface settings, noting that performance is bounded by mesh convergence of training data, and this nuance is a useful contribution in itself.

The cross-dataset experiment (Table 6) is a genuine demonstration that a mesh-agnostic architecture can transfer simulation knowledge across incompatible mesh structures, which is a practically valuable capability for building subsurface surrogates.
weaknesses: The central architectural contribution is thin. APT is an assembly of existing components (Perceiver cross-attention, GNO radius graphs, DiT conditioning, PerceiverIO-style decoding), and the authors themselves acknowledge gated fusion has been explored before (Wen et al., 2022; Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024), arguing only that it is now applied to the latent token space. The gate in Eq. (1) is a simple learned scalar gate. This incremental novelty is not adequately supported by ablations.

The ablations undercut the headline claim. In Table 1, APT (local only) achieves 0.18/0.36 vs. 0.11/0.32 for fused, with overlapping error bars; in Table 3, 0.014 vs. 0.011 (both ±0.01); in Table 14, fused (0.9107) vs. TFNO baseline (0.9079). The fusion mechanism - presented as the key innovation - yields marginal and often statistically indistinguishable gains. No significance testing is provided.

Baseline fairness is questionable. Grid-based baselines require interpolation onto regular grids (inherently handicapped on irregular/adaptive meshes), the flagship adaptive-mesh ATES comparison has no competitive direct baseline (MGN 'fails to make prediction'), and point-cloud models (Transolver, AB-UPT) that could plausibly handle adaptive meshes were never tested on it. The 'first to learn from adaptive meshes' claim is thus not verified against the most obvious competitors.

APT is trained with direct one-step conditioning on the target time t, while baselines like MGN-LSTM are autoregressive. This confounds comparisons in Tables 1 and 10, sidesteps rollout error accumulation that baselines suffer, and leaves long-horizon rollout stability - essential for practical deployment - undemonstrated.

Super-resolution evidence is weak. The CarBench result in Table 5 (top) is based on 'a representative unseen test sample' (a single case), and on the full CarBench test set (Table 13) APT ranks second (96.00 ± 3.1 vs. AB-UPT's 96.75 ± 0.19) with anomalously large variance attributed to a re-implementation of the protocol. The abstract's claim of 'robust super-resolution capabilities' is contradicted by the paper's own nuanced Section 4.1.
Speedup figures are inflated by hardware mismatch: simulators run on single-core (Table 10) or 20-core (Table 12) CPUs while APT runs on A100 GPUs.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance: code and all three newly created datasets (ATES, wastewater, channelized) are only promised 'upon publication', so none of the novel claims can currently be verified.

The manuscript has numerous typos, grammatical errors, and internal inconsistencies (e.g., text states APT takes 0.05s in Table 10 discussion while the table reports 0.017s; 'apt... to directly on the raw' (Sec 3.3); 'This is introduces' (Sec 2.3); 'Channalized'; missing glyphs in Figure 9), suggesting insufficient polish for a main-track submission.

strengths: Broad and well-designed empirical evaluation across seven benchmark datasets spanning structured grids, unstructured meshes, nested LGR, and dynamically adaptive (DMO) meshes, covering diverse physics (single-phase, multiphase, compositional flow, heat transfer) and scales from thousands to millions of cells.

The demonstration of direct learning from time-varying adaptive meshes (ATES/DMO benchmark, Section 3.3) addresses a genuine and previously unserved gap; grid- and graph-based baselines genuinely cannot handle this setting, and the 4x error improvement over interpolated baselines is convincing.

Careful and unusually honest treatment of super-resolution: the paper distinguishes architectural mesh-invariance from training-data fidelity and explicitly cautions that ATES degradation (1.8%) reflects mesh convergence limits of the training data rather than the architecture (Section 4.1). This is a mature, credible discussion.

Useful ablation studies (global-only vs. local-only vs. fused) that support the central design claim, and a cross-dataset training experiment (R^2 32.0% -> 86.7%) that concretely demonstrates the practical value of mesh-agnostic pre-training.

Exceptional reproducibility detail in the appendix: full training costs, GPU memory, throughput, hyperparameters, dataset generation details, and inference runtime comparisons (Tables 7, 8, 10, 12); the promised release of datasets and code upon publication is a positive.
Strong practical impact framing: ~6,800x speedup over ECLIPSE with 97% fewer parameters than Nested-FNO is a meaningful result for the subsurface energy domain.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is incremental. The model is a composition of well-known components (Perceiver cross-attention encoder, GNO local branch, DiT-style blocks, gated fusion). The authors themselves acknowledge gated fusion exists in prior hybrid operators (Wen et al., 2022; Liu & Tang, 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024) and position the contribution as 'using fusion to construct the latent token space' — a thin distinction that needs stronger justification or analysis (e.g., learned gate statistics) to be convincing.

Missing key baselines on the subsurface benchmarks. The paper criticizes UPT and Transolver-family architectures in the introduction but never compares against them on the faulted CO2 or ATES tasks (Table 1 and Table 3 only include U-Net, U-FNO, MGN, MGN-LSTM). Given that these are the closest architectural relatives, their absence weakens the 'outperforms SOTA' claim.

Comparison framing is potentially unfair: APT is trained with direct one-step temporal conditioning while MGN-LSTM uses autoregressive rollout with error accumulation (Section 2.6, C.1.2). A direct-prediction MGN variant or an error-accumulation analysis is needed to attribute gains to the architecture rather than the training scheme.

Selective reporting in the super-resolution evaluation. The CarBench 'mesh-convergent behavior' claim (Table 5, top) is based on a single representative test sample, while the full-test-set results (Table 13) show APT (R^2 96.00 +/- 3.1, Rel L2 0.1535 +/- 0.038) clearly below AB-UPT (96.75 +/- 0.19, 0.1358 +/- 0.0024) with ~20x larger variance and worse latency/memory. The abstract's 'outperforms state-of-the-art' framing overstates this outcome.

The fusion ablation gains are small and inconsistent across tasks: on the faulted CO2 dataset, local-only achieves 0.18%/0.36% vs. fused 0.11%/0.32% (Table 1), and on ATES 0.014 vs. 0.011 (Table 3), suggesting the local GNO branch carries most of the performance; the marginal value of the global branch and gating deserves more scrutiny (e.g., statistical significance of differences).

No physics-based evaluation: no mass-conservation checks, plume-volume or front-location errors, or long-horizon rollout analysis despite the emphasis on sharp fronts and long-range pressure propagation; the relative L2/plume-error metrics alone may hide systematic bias relevant to downstream decision-making.
Code and data are only promised 'upon publication'; at submission time neither is verifiable, which limits reproducibility assessment despite the thorough appendix.

Presentation issues: numerous grammatical errors ('This design is introduces', 'allows it to directly on the raw', 'dataest', 'A essential challenge'), and some claims (e.g., 'first neural operator to learn directly from adaptive mesh datasets') are stated as definitive without qualification.

strengths: Genuinely new capability: APT appears to be the first neural operator trained end-to-end directly on HR-adaptive (DMO) simulation data with time-varying mesh topology (ATES benchmark), avoiding interpolation error that penalizes grid-based and fixed-topology baselines — a meaningful and well-motivated contribution for subsurface modeling.

Breadth and rigor of empirical evaluation: five distinct benchmarks spanning structured, unstructured (PEBI with faults), nested LGR (up to 1M cells), adaptive, and cross-domain meshes, plus standard PDE benchmarks (Airfoil, Darcy, Elasticity) in Appendix D, with detailed training configurations, hyperparameters, and compute costs provided (Tables 8-9, Appendix C).

Honest and nuanced discussion: the super-resolution section (4.1) candidly distinguishes 'architectural mesh-invariance' from training-data fidelity, and the ATES degradation result is interpreted responsibly; limitations (single-physics scaling only, no fine-tuning across physics) are acknowledged.

Valuable system-level experiments beyond accuracy: cross-dataset joint training (R2 on channelized task improves 32.0% -> 86.7%), data/model scaling curves, OOD generalization to unseen geostatistical models, and Pareto-front accuracy/efficiency analysis with 6,800x+ speedup over ECLIPSE.

Comprehensive ablations of global-only, local-only, and fused variants across most benchmarks, and an unusually detailed appendix enabling reproducibility (mesh generation, governing equations, baseline adaptations).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the method is essentially a Perceiver cross-attention encoder (Jaegle et al.) fused with a GNO encoder via a learned scalar gate, followed by DiT blocks and a cross-attention decoder — each component is well-established, and gated local-global fusion has been explored before (the paper concedes Wen et al. 2022, Liu & Tang 2025); the claimed novelty ('uniquely employs fused representations to construct the latent token space') is a thin conceptual distinction.

The central claim that fused attention is critical is only weakly supported by the ablations: on the faulted CO2 benchmark local-only nearly matches fused (0.18 vs 0.11 pressure; 0.36 vs 0.32 saturation), and on ATES the fused gain (0.011 vs 0.014) is within the reported standard deviations; on CarBench fused and non-fused are nearly identical. The paper's narrative of complementary local-global inductive biases is plausible but not decisively demonstrated.

Not always SOTA: on CarBench APT ranks second behind AB-UPT (96.00 vs 96.75 R2), and UPT is faster (0.001s vs 0.002s); the strongest empirical case rests on the new ATES dataset and the LGR benchmark, where baselines are either interpolated or memory-limited.

Some experimental fairness concerns: grid baselines on faulted CO2 and ATES must interpolate unstructured data onto regular grids, which the paper itself argues introduces smoothing artifacts — this stacks the deck in favor of mesh-native APT on those comparisons; CarBench evaluation used a re-implemented protocol with acknowledged deviations.

Presentation issues: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('is introduces', 'A essential challenge', 'dataest', 'Channalized', 'perfromance'), minor numerical inconsistencies between text and tables (0.30% vs 0.32% saturation in Table 2), and inconsistently formatted parameter counts (1.2M vs 1.38M vs 1.36M across Table 1 and appendix text).

The direct one-step (initial-condition-to-query-time) training paradigm, while avoiding rollout error accumulation, sidesteps evaluation of long-horizon autoregressive stability, which is a key practical criterion for many neural PDE surrogates and how several baselines (MGN, MGN-LSTM) are actually used.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across seven datasets spanning structured, unstructured, adaptive/nested meshes, multiple physics types (multiphase flow, heat transport), and scales from thousands to a million cells; this breadth is unusual and valuable for the subsurface ML community.

The demonstration of learning directly from HR-adaptive (DMO) simulation data with time-varying mesh topology (ATES benchmark) is a genuine and practically important capability that most neural operators cannot handle without interpolation.

Honest treatment of super-resolution: the paper explicitly distinguishes mesh-invariance of the architecture from mesh convergence of the training data and cautions against over-claiming super-resolution in subsurface settings; this nuanced discussion (Section 4.1) is commendable.

Ablation studies (local-only, global-only, fused) are included on several benchmarks and generally support the central design claim, and scaling/cross-dataset experiments probe the foundation-model motivation beyond headline accuracy.
Supplementary material is thorough: governing equations, mesh generation, training configurations, training costs, and inference timing tables for baselines and APT.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: APT is essentially a composition of well-known components — Perceiver cross-attention (Jaegle et al.), GNO/message passing (Li et al., Hamilton et al.), a learnable gate already used in prior hybrid operators (Wen et al., 2022; Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024), and DiT-style modulation (Peebles & Xie). The claimed novelty (gating used for latent-token construction rather than decoding) is incremental and the paper itself concedes gated fusion exists in prior work; a sharper conceptual contribution is needed for a main-track ML venue.

Some central empirical claims are weaker than stated. On Table 1, the local-only variant (0.18% δP, 0.36% δSg) is nearly as good as the fused model (0.11%, 0.32%), so the fused mechanism's value is marginal on the flagship benchmark. On ATES, fused vs. non-fused differs by 0.003 with ±0.01 standard deviations. On CarBench (Table 14), APT is not the best model (AB-UPT is), and on the homogeneous PDE benchmarks (Table 17) APT consistently trails Transolver. The narrative of consistent SOTA superiority is thus overstated relative to the evidence.

Presentation quality is below the bar: numerous grammatical errors throughout ('This design is introduces', 'frequently interpolation', 'A essential challenge', 'perfromance gain', 'can not be reused'), inconsistent notation and naming, and citations formatted oddly (e.g., 'Wen et al., 2023b' colored as if unresolved). This suggests insufficient polish for a camera-ready-quality submission.

Baseline fairness is not always clear. Grid-based baselines for the faulted CO2 benchmark require interpolation, and the tabulated comparison mixes direct predictors with autoregressive models under different protocols; the advantages of APT partly conflate mesh handling with evaluation regime. The CarBench comparison used a self-reproduced protocol rather than the official codebase, and the authors acknowledge larger variance in their numbers.

Reproducibility is uncertain: code and newly created datasets are only promised 'upon publication', with no repository, and key details (e.g., exact DMO/ATES preprocessing, anchor supernode construction) are described only at a high level.

The 'first architecture to learn directly from adaptive mesh / DMO datasets' claim is strong and difficult to verify; given R-adaptive-capable methods exist, the claim should be more carefully scoped and justified against a broader related-work survey.

The title and framing advertise a 'physics' transformer, but the model is physics-agnostic in the sense that no physical structure (conservation, symmetry, PDE priors) is encoded; this framing may mislead readers about the method's nature.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across seven benchmarks spanning structured, unstructured, nested-LGR, and fully HR-adaptive (DMO) meshes, multiple physics regimes (single/multiphase, compositional, heat transport), and scales from thousands to millions of cells — far more thorough than typical architecture papers.

The demonstration of direct learning from HR-adaptive/DMO simulations (ATES, Section 3.3) with time-varying mesh topology is a genuinely new capability for neural operators, and the 2.2x/3.6x error reduction over Transolver/UPT on that benchmark is substantive.

Useful ablations (local-only vs. global-only vs. fused) reported consistently across multiple benchmarks (Tables 1, 3, 4, 5, 15), which supports the central claim that fusing local and global pathways matters for heterogeneous subsurface media.

Several sections show scientific maturity: the super-resolution analysis (Section 4.1) honestly distinguishes architectural mesh-invariance from training-data mesh convergence and warns against overclaiming; the CarBench appendix candidly reports protocol reproduction issues and that APT is second-best to AB-UPT; the limitations section explicitly states scaling results cover only one physics type.

Cross-dataset training (Table 6: R2 32.0% -> 86.7% on the data-limited channelized task) and data/model scaling experiments (Table 7) provide evidence toward the foundation-model-backbone positioning.

Baselines generally include recent mesh-native transformers (UPT, Transolver, MINO, HOOD, AB-UPT) with matched parameter counts on some tasks, and detailed training configurations and cost tables (Tables 8, 9) are provided.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is modest. The gated fusion of local graph and global Perceiver pathways (Eq. 1) is acknowledged by the authors to exist in prior hybrid operators (Wen et al., 2022; Liu & Tang, 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al., 2024); the claimed distinction ('uniquely employs fused representations to construct the latent token space') is thin. The remaining components (Perceiver encoder, GNO, DiT blocks with adaLN-style modulation, cross-attention decoder) are all established, so the contribution is largely an application/domain-driven combination rather than a new operator design.

The direct one-step training scheme (conditioning on initial state and query time t) creates a potential comparability asymmetry: APT avoids autoregressive error accumulation entirely, while several baselines (MGN-LSTM, fixed-grid U-Net/FNO rollouts) are evaluated autoregressively. The paper does not disentangle whether APT's advantage stems from the fused architecture or from the easier one-step task; an autoregressive or sequential variant of APT would strengthen the architectural claims.

Some baseline fairness concerns: on ATES, UPT and Transolver were trained for only 50 epochs (Appendix C.2.1) while APT's protocol uses more epochs and larger conditioning capacity; hyperparameter tuning effort per baseline is not documented uniformly, making the 2-4x error-gap claims harder to attribute purely to architecture.

The 'first neural operator to learn directly from adaptive mesh datasets' priority claim is strong and difficult to verify; it should be softened or better supported against adjacent work on adaptive/remeshable discretizations.

Evidence of statistical rigor is uneven: Table 3 reports ±0.01 on what appears to be a single run, and some key comparisons (e.g., APT fused 0.11% vs. local-only 0.18% pressure error in Table 1) have overlapping or near-overlapping uncertainty ranges, so some claimed improvements are small relative to variance.

Presentation quality is rough for a main-track submission: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('dataest', 'Channalized', 'perfromance', 'A essential challenge', '3.67,GB'), a subscript error in Eq. (15)-(16) description ('p ∈ {a, g} indexes the aqueous (g) and gas (g) phases'), and occasional awkward phrasing that requires re-reading.
Code and the newly created datasets are only promised 'upon publication', so reproducibility currently rests on appendix descriptions alone.
